CALIFORNIA DATA BROKER REGISTRATION ACT (DELETE ACT) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc. · privacy@acme.com or (415) 555-0100

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Data Broker Registration Act Information Sheet describes California's Data Broker Registration Act, Civil Code § 1798.99.80 et seq., as amended by the Delete Act (Stats. 2023, Ch. 709 (SB 362)) and by Stats. 2025, Ch. 466 (SB 361). It is prepared in connection with Acme, Inc.'s data practices and is intended as background alongside, not a substitute for, Acme, Inc.'s separate California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA/CPRA) materials. The Data Broker Registration Act is a distinct, additional statutory scheme from the CCPA: the CCPA generally governs a covered business's collection, use, and sale of personal information regardless of the business's relationship to the consumer, while the Data Broker Registration Act imposes separate annual registration, fee, and deletion-platform obligations that apply specifically to a "data broker" as that term is defined in Civil Code § 1798.99.80(c) — a category of business defined, in part, by the absence of a direct relationship with the consumer whose information it collects and sells. A business can be subject to the CCPA without meeting the Data Broker Registration Act's narrower "data broker" definition, and a business that does meet that definition is subject to both statutory schemes at once. Questions about Acme, Inc.'s data collection and disclosure practices may be directed as follows: privacy@acme.com or (415) 555-0100.

THE STATUTORY DEFINITION OF "DATA BROKER," AND ITS EXEMPTIONS
California's Data Broker Registration Act defines "data broker" to mean a business that knowingly collects and sells to third parties the personal information of a consumer with whom the business does not have a direct relationship. The absence of a direct relationship between the business and the consumer is the element that separates a "data broker" under this Act from a business more generally subject to the CCPA, which is not limited to businesses lacking a direct consumer relationship. The statute defines "data broker" to exclude four categories of entities, each only to the extent the entity is actually covered by the referenced other law: (1) an entity to the extent it is covered by the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act; (2) an entity to the extent it is covered by the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act and its implementing regulations; (3) an entity to the extent it is covered by California's Insurance Information and Privacy Protection Act; and (4) an entity, or a business associate of a covered entity, to the extent its processing of personal information is exempt under Civil Code § 1798.146 (the CCPA's own exemption for entities and information governed by the Confidentiality of Medical Information Act or HIPAA).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(c) “Data broker” means a business that knowingly collects and sells to third parties the personal information of a consumer with whom the business does not have a direct relationship. “Data broker” does not include any of the following:"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.99.80(c) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text, as amended by Stats. 2023, Ch. 709 (SB 362)), Data Broker Registration Act, definition of "data broker" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1798.99.80.)
  "(1) An entity to the extent that it is covered by the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act (15 U.S.C. Sec. 1681 et seq.). (2) An entity to the extent that it is covered by the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (Public Law 106-102) and implementing regulations. (3) An entity to the extent that it is covered by the Insurance Information and Privacy Protection Act (Article 6.6 (commencing with Section 791) of Chapter 1 of Part 2 of Division 1 of the Insurance Code). For purposes of this paragraph, “business associate” and “covered entity” have the same meanings as defined in Section 1798.146."
  — Cal. Civ. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Data Broker Registration Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific business. This clause states the statutory definition and exemption categories; it does not determine whether any specific business (i) knowingly collects and sells personal information, (ii) has or lacks a "direct relationship" with the consumers whose information it sells, or (iii) actually falls within one of the four exemption categories for its own operations — those are fact-specific determinations this document does not make. Civil Code § 1798.99.80(a) also incorporates the CCPA's own definitions from Section 1798.140 (for terms such as "business," "sell," "personal information," and "consumer") except where this title specifies otherwise; those incorporated CCPA definitions were not independently re-quoted here and are addressed in this corpus's separate CCPA documents. No case law was checked on this provision; the statute's own text is unambiguous, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

ANNUAL REGISTRATION WITH THE CALIFORNIA PRIVACY PROTECTION AGENCY, AND THE REGISTRATION FEE
Under the current text of the Data Broker Registration Act, a business that meets the statutory definition of "data broker" for a given year must register with the California Privacy Protection Agency ("CPPA") on or before January 31 of the following year. The CPPA, not the California Attorney General, is the agency currently named in the statute as the registering authority; the CPPA also administers the "Data Brokers' Registry Fund" created in the State Treasury, into which registration fees, penalties, and other amounts collected under this title are deposited. As part of registering, a data broker must pay a registration fee, in an amount the CPPA determines, that may not exceed the reasonable costs of establishing and maintaining the CPPA's public data-broker informational website and the reasonable costs of establishing, maintaining, and providing access to the accessible deletion mechanism described elsewhere in this title.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]

Registration fees shall be deposited in the Data Brokers’ Registry Fund, created within the State Treasury pursuant to Section 1798.99.81, and used for the purposes outlined in this paragraph."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.99.82(b)(1) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text, as amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 466 (SB 361)), Data Broker Registration Act, registration fee (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1798.99.82.)

The currently codified text names the California Privacy Protection Agency, not the Attorney General, as the registering and fee-setting authority; this document did not independently verify or trace the legislative history of that change from the statute's original 2019 enactment (which predates the Agency's creation) through the Delete Act's 2023 amendments — a reader interested in that history should consult the amendment notes on the statute's own text or the bill history for SB 362, which are outside the scope of what this clause verifies. This clause does not state the specific dollar amount of any registration fee the CPPA has actually set, since the statute leaves that amount to the Agency's own determination rather than fixing it in the statutory text itself, and this document did not independently verify a current fee schedule. No case law was checked on this provision; the statute's own text is unambiguous, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

INFORMATION A DATA BROKER'S REGISTRATION MUST INCLUDE
Beyond paying the registration fee, the Data Broker Registration Act requires a registering data broker to provide the CPPA with specific information as part of registration, including: the data broker's name and its primary physical, email, and internet website addresses; metrics the data broker separately compiles about consumer requests it receives and how it responds to them; whether it collects personal information of minors; whether it collects specific categories of sensitive information such as government-issued identification numbers, biometric data, precise geolocation, citizenship or immigration status, union membership, sexual orientation, gender identity, or reproductive health care data; whether it has shared or sold consumer data to a foreign actor, the federal government, other state governments, law enforcement, or a developer of a generative artificial intelligence system or model in the past year; a link to a webpage, free of dark patterns, describing how consumers may exercise their existing CCPA rights to delete, correct, know, opt out of sale or sharing, and limit use of sensitive personal information; and whether and to what extent the data broker or its subsidiaries are also regulated under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, California's Insurance Information and Privacy Protection Act, or federal/state medical-information confidentiality laws (HIPAA and the Confidentiality of Medical Information Act).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]

(D) Whether the data broker collects consumers’ names, dates of birth, ZIP Codes, email addresses, or phone numbers. (F) Whether the data broker collects consumers’ drivers’ license number, California identification card number, tax identification number, social security number, passport number, military identification number, or other unique identification number issued on a government document commonly used to verify the identity of a specific individual. (G) Whether the data broker collects consumers’ mobile advertising identification numbers, connected television identification numbers, or vehicle identification numbers (VIN). (J) Whether the data broker collects consumers’ sexual orientation status. (K) Whether the data broker collects consumers’ gender identity and gender expression data. (L) Whether the data broker collects consumers’ biometric data. (M) Whether the data broker collects consumers’ precise geolocation. (N) Whether the data broker collects consumers’ reproductive health care data. (O) Whether the data broker has shared or sold consumers’ data to a foreign actor in the past year. (P) Whether the data broker has shared or sold consumers’ data to the federal government in the past year. (Q) Whether the data broker has shared or sold consumers’ data to other state governments in the past year. (R) Whether the data broker has shared or sold consumers’ data to law enforcement in the past year, unless that data was shared pursuant to a subpoena or court order. (S) Whether the data broker has shared or sold consumers’ data to a developer of a GenAI system or model in the past year. (T) Up to three, but no fewer than one, of the most common types of personal information that the data broker collects, if the data broker does not collect the information described in subparagraphs (D) and (G). (U) Beginning January 1, 2029, whether the data broker has undergone an audit as described in subdivision (e) of Section 1798.99.86, and, if so, the most recent year that the data broker has submitted a report resulting from the audit and any related materials to the California Privacy Protection Agency. (V) A link to a page on the data broker’s internet website that does both of the following: (i) Details how consumers may exercise their privacy rights by doing all of the following: (I) Deleting personal information, as described in Section 1798.105. (II) Correcting inaccurate personal information, as described in Section 1798.106. (III) Learning what personal information is being collected and how to access that personal information, as described in Section 1798.110. (IV) Learning what personal information is being sold or shared and to whom, as described in Section 1798.115. (V) Learning how to opt out of the sale or sharing of personal information, as described in Section 1798.120. (VI) Learning how to limit the use and disclosure of sensitive personal information, as described in Section 1798.121. (ii) Does not make use of any dark patterns. (ii) The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (Public Law 106-102) and implementing regulations. (iii) The Insurance Information and Privacy Protection Act (Article 6.6 (commencing with Section 791) of Chapter 1 of Part 2 of Division 1 of the Insurance Code). (iv) The Confidentiality of Medical Information Act (Part 2.6 (commencing with Section 56) of Division 1) or the privacy, security, and breach notification rules issued by the United States Department of Health and Human Services, Parts 160 and 164 of Title 45 of the Code of Federal Regulations, established pursuant to the federal Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (Public Law 104-191). THE DELETE REQUEST AND OPT-OUT PLATFORM ("DROP"), AND ITS PHASED COMPLIANCE DEADLINES
The Delete Act's central new mechanism, commonly referred to as "DROP" (the Delete Request and Opt-out Platform), is an accessible deletion mechanism the statute directs the CPPA to establish. The statute set January 1, 2026, as the deadline for the CPPA to establish this mechanism. As designed, the mechanism must let a consumer submit a single, verifiable request that every registered data broker holding that consumer's personal information delete it, while also allowing the consumer to selectively exclude specific data brokers from that single request, and to request an alteration of a prior request after at least 45 days have passed. Separately, the statute sets August 1, 2026, as the date beginning which a registered data broker must access the mechanism at least once every 45 days and, within 45 days of receiving a deletion request through it, process and complete the deletion of the requesting consumer's personal information (subject to statutory exceptions the mechanism itself administers). As of the September 4, 2026 date of this information sheet's preparation, both the January 1, 2026 platform-establishment deadline and the August 1, 2026 data-broker compliance-start deadline set out in the current statutory text have already passed.

ADMINISTRATIVE FINES FOR FAILING TO REGISTER OR FAILING TO COMPLY WITH DROP
The Data Broker Registration Act's current text provides two separate administrative fine schemes, both enforced by the California Privacy Protection Agency through an administrative action. First, a data broker that fails to register as the statute requires is liable for an administrative fine of $200 for each day it fails to register, plus an amount equal to the registration fees that were due during the period of nonregistration, plus the CPPA's reasonable investigation and administration expenses. Second, and separately, a data broker required to register that fails to comply with the DROP-related deletion requirements of Civil Code § 1798.99.86 is liable for an administrative fine of $200 for each deletion request, for each day the data broker fails to delete the information as that section requires, plus the CPPA's reasonable investigation and administration expenses. All penalties, fines, fees, and expenses recovered under either scheme are deposited into the Data Brokers' Registry Fund.

(2) An amount equal to the fees that were due during the period it failed to register. (3) Reasonable expenses incurred by the California Privacy Protection Agency in the investigation and administration of the action."
  — Cal. Civ.   "(d) A data broker required to register under this title that fails to comply with the requirements of Section 1798.99.86 is liable for administrative fines and costs in an administrative action brought by the California Privacy Protection Agency as follows: (1) An administrative fine of two hundred dollars ($200) for each deletion request for each day the data broker fails to delete information as required by Section 1798.99.86. (2) Reasonable expenses incurred by the California Privacy Protection Agency in the investigation and administration of the action."
  — Cal. Civ. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Data Broker Registration Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific business, and not a claim that any specific business has, or has not, incurred any fine described here. This clause does not address any other enforcement mechanism that might separately apply to conduct also covered by the general CCPA (such as CCPA-specific Attorney General or CPPA enforcement actions), which this document's companion CCPA documents address separately, nor does it verify whether the CPPA has actually brought any administrative action of the kind described. expectedJSON.body: Beyond paying the registration fee, the Data Broker Registration Act requires a registering data broker to provide the CPPA with specific information as part of registration, including: the data broker's name and its primary physical, email, and internet website addresses; metrics the data broker separately compiles about consumer requests it receives and how it responds to them; whether it collects personal information of minors; whether it collects specific categories of sensitive information such as government-issued identification numbers, biometric data, precise geolocation, citizenship or immigration status, union membership, sexual orientation, gender identity, or reproductive health care data; whether it has shared or sold consumer data to a foreign actor, the federal government, other state governments, law enforcement, or a developer of a generative artificial intelligence system or model in the past year; a link to a webpage, free of dark patterns, describing how consumers may exercise their existing CCPA rights to delete, correct, know, opt out of sale or sharing, and limit use of sensitive personal information; and whether and to what extent the data broker or its subsidiaries are also regulated under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, California's Insurance Information and Privacy Protection Act, or federal/state medical-information confidentiality laws (HIPAA and the Confidentiality of Medical Information Act).

citations.quote: (2) Provide the following information: (A) The name of the data broker and its primary physical, email, and internet website addresses. (B) The metrics compiled pursuant to paragraphs (1) and (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 1798.99.85. (C) Whether the data broker collects the personal information of minors. (D) Whether the data broker collects consumers’ names, dates of birth, ZIP Codes, email addresses, or phone numbers. (E) Whether the data broker collects consumers’ account login or account number in combination with any required security code, access code, or password that would permit access to a consumer’s account with a third party. (F) Whether the data broker collects consumers’ drivers’ license number, California identification card number, tax identification number, social security number, passport number, military identification number, or other unique identification number issued on a government document commonly used to verify the identity of a specific individual. (G) Whether the data broker collects consumers’ mobile advertising identification numbers, connected television identification numbers, or vehicle identification numbers (VIN). (H) Whether the data broker collects consumers’ citizenship data, including immigration status. (I) Whether the data broker collects consumers’ union membership status. (J) Whether the data broker collects consumers’ sexual orientation status. (K) Whether the data broker collects consumers’ gender identity and gender expression data. (L) Whether the data broker collects consumers’ biometric data. (M) Whether the data broker collects consumers’ precise geolocation. (N) Whether the data broker collects consumers’ reproductive health care data. (O) Whether the data broker has shared or sold consumers’ data to a foreign actor in the past year. (P) Whether the data broker has shared or sold consumers’ data to the federal government in the past year. (Q) Whether the data broker has shared or sold consumers’ data to other state governments in the past year. (R) Whether the data broker has shared or sold consumers’ data to law enforcement in the past year, unless that data was shared pursuant to a subpoena or court order. (S) Whether the data broker has shared or sold consumers’ data to a developer of a GenAI system or model in the past year. (T) Up to three, but no fewer than one, of the most common types of personal information that the data broker collects, if the data broker does not collect the information described in subparagraphs (D) and (G). (U) Beginning January 1, 2029, whether the data broker has undergone an audit as described in subdivision (e) of Section 1798.99.86, and, if so, the most recent year that the data broker has submitted a report resulting from the audit and any related materials to the California Privacy Protection Agency. (V) A link to a page on the data broker’s internet website that does both of the following: (i) Details how consumers may exercise their privacy rights by doing all of the following: (I) Deleting personal information, as described in Section 1798.105. (II) Correcting inaccurate personal information, as described in Section 1798.106. (III) Learning what personal information is being collected and how to access that personal information, as described in Section 1798.110. (IV) Learning what personal information is being sold or shared and to whom, as described in Section 1798.115. (V) Learning how to opt out of the sale or sharing of personal information, as described in Section 1798.120. (VI) Learning how to limit the use and disclosure of sensitive personal information, as described in Section 1798.121. (ii) Does not make use of any dark patterns. (W) Whether and to what extent the data broker or any of its subsidiaries is regulated by any of the following: (i) The federal Fair Credit Reporting Act (15 U.S.C. Sec. 1681 et seq.). (ii) The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (Public Law 106-102) and implementing regulations. (iii) The Insurance Information and Privacy Protection Act (Article 6.6 (commencing with Section 791) of Chapter 1 of Part 2 of Division 1 of the Insurance Code). (iv) The Confidentiality of Medical Information Act (Part 2.6 (commencing with Section 56) of Division 1) or the privacy, security, and breach notification rules issued by the United States Department of Health and Human Services, Parts 160 and 164 of Title 45 of the Code of Federal Regulations, established pursuant to the federal Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (Public Law 104-191). (X) Any additional information or explanation the data broker chooses to provide concerning its data collection practices.

expectedJSON.body: The Delete Act's central new mechanism, commonly referred to as "DROP" (the Delete Request and Opt-out Platform), is an accessible deletion mechanism the statute directs the CPPA to establish. The statute set January 1, 2026, as the deadline for the CPPA to establish this mechanism. As designed, the mechanism must let a consumer submit a single, verifiable request that every registered data broker holding that consumer's personal information delete it, while also allowing the consumer to selectively exclude specific data brokers from that single request, and to request an alteration of a prior request after at least 45 days have passed. Separately, the statute sets August 1, 2026, as the date beginning which a registered data broker must access the mechanism at least once every 45 days and, within 45 days of receiving a deletion request through it, process and complete the deletion of the requesting consumer's personal information (subject to statutory exceptions the mechanism itself administers). As of the September 4, 2026 date of this information sheet's preparation, both the January 1, 2026 platform-establishment deadline and the August 1, 2026 data-broker compliance-start deadline set out in the current statutory text have already passed.

expectedJSON.body: The Data Broker Registration Act's current text provides two separate administrative fine schemes, both enforced by the California Privacy Protection Agency through an administrative action. First, a data broker that fails to register as the statute requires is liable for an administrative fine of $200 for each day it fails to register, plus an amount equal to the registration fees that were due during the period of nonregistration, plus the CPPA's reasonable investigation and administration expenses. Second, and separately, a data broker required to register that fails to comply with the DROP-related deletion requirements of Civil Code § 1798.99.86 is liable for an administrative fine of $200 for each deletion request, for each day the data broker fails to delete the information as that section requires, plus the CPPA's reasonable investigation and administration expenses. All penalties, fines, fees, and expenses recovered under either scheme are deposited into the Data Brokers' Registry Fund.

citations.quote: (c) A data broker that fails to register as required by this section is liable for administrative fines and costs in an administrative action brought by the California Privacy Protection Agency as follows: (1) An administrative fine of two hundred dollars ($200) for each day the data broker fails to register as required by this section. (2) An amount equal to the fees that were due during the period it failed to register. (3) Reasonable expenses incurred by the California Privacy Protection Agency in the investigation and administration of the action.

(2) Reasonable expenses incurred by the California Privacy Protection Agency in the investigation and administration of the action.
